subject: Re: Setting up a project with many datasets and many covariates

messages.author: 06199470668a2843
messages.subject: Re: Setting up a project with many datasets and many covariates
parts:
Hi Tiago,

thank you very much for these guidelines! This should offer a good deal o=
f
simplification.
> > (note: I'm missing how you got 2048 models below, as 2 key * 3
adjustments* 64 covariate combinations (which means no interaction terms
and all possibilities from no to 6 covariates) =3D384, and there is no
number which multiplied by it leads to 2048 - I might be missing
something rather obvious!)

My bad - that number was from an earlier assessment involving more
covariates, and kind of stuck due to its lovely 2^ nature.
384 models is correct, of course.

> > 1. There seems to be no way to simplify at the species level, so you
should need to deal with a separate analysis by species. Species could
be considered a covariate too, though there's probably no advantage in
doing so (unless sample size is small for some of the species - see
MATHEW W. ALLDREDGE, KENNETH H. POLLOCK, THEODORE R. SIMONS, SUSAN A.
SHRINER (2007) Multiple-species analysis of point count data: a more
parsimonious modelling framework Journal of Applied Ecology 44 (2) ,
281=96290 for details).

If I understand their approach correctly, a model including a species
covariate was created with a pooled data set for a "species group", then
that model was used to produce estimates for each individual species usin=
g
detections of that species only. Among my few focal species, there are
only two that could be grouped that way (blackbirds and thrushes), and I
will give it a try with these in addition to individual models and see if
it is advantageous.

> > 2. You might abstain from using all the combinations of key functions +
adjustment terms. Just try one of the adjustment terms (say cosine) and
then proceed. At the end you can do some exploratory EDA to see if
others would lead to substantial differences, I predict not. So you cut
the number of models to try by a factor of 3.
> >
> > 3. Try each covariate alone (with both key functions), and see if there
is some that look much more promising than others. Focus on those. It is
unlikely that after using the 2 our 3 that most help explaining the
detection function you still need the remaining 4 or 3. Also, it might
be the case that overall one of the key functions starts looking more
promising than the other. If that is not the case then you might need
some model averaging in the end. The advantage in the Auk paper you
refer was that despite having different AIC's, different models were all
leading to very similar density estimates, so the choice of model was
less influential in the final result.

Thanks, that was exactly the area I was unsure about! So some judicious
stepwise addition might save me a lot of work.
I was planning to do some model averaging in any case to check how the
average compares to the top few models.

> > 4. Do you expect that detection probability will change by area? Is it
worth to include area as an additional covariate (say as a factor; it
depends on sample size if you actually can estimate all the parameters
involved), rather than treating it as a separate analysis by area?

The areas are individual farms that are spread over a large area and vary
from stroll-through-pastures to abseil-through-bush (well almost :), so I
feel different detection probabilities are to be expected. I am also
aiming for a comparison of different geographical "farm clusters". I
therefore think separate analyses will be useful.

thanks for your help!
cheers
florian

> >
> >
> >
> > Florian Weller wrote:
>> >> Hi List,
>> >>
>> >> I am engaged in setting up the analysis structure for a Distance proje=
ct
>> >> in which the data will have to be analysed in 16 distinct geographic
>> >> parcels, for each of 4 species. I am wondering what approach to use to
>> >> keep the number of candidate models at manageable levels when
>> >> investigating different key functions, adjustments, and covariates.
>> >>
>> >> My data are for bird sightings on farms over two years, and I would li=
ke
>> >> to try out a variety of promising covariates. The problem is that I se=
e
>> >> the numbers of models ballooning enormously. If I were to assess all
>> >> possible combinations for a single species in a single area, I would g=
et
>> >>
>> >> (2 key functions [halfnormal, hazard]) * (3 adjustment terms [cos, sim=
,
>> >> her]) * (permutations of 6 covariates)
>> >> =3D 2048 models
>> >>
>> >> Seeing that I would have to repeat THAT 64 times (for 4 species in 16
>> >> areas), this brute force approach obviously won't work. But I have a h=
ard
>> >> time deciding where to simplify.
>> >> In my first attempt, I tried to find a good "base model" for each set,
>> >> just a key function + adjustment, without any covariates. Having selec=
ted
>> >> that, I then ran the 64 covariate permutations on this model, which is
>> >> manageable. But I've developed some doubt about the validity of this
>> >> approach. E.g., in the 2007 Auk paper by Marques et al. (Table 2), a
>> >> similar permutative approach suggests that in a ranking of models with
>> >> different key models, adjustment terms, and covariates, the same covar=
iate
>> >> combination with a different key model or adjustment choice can lead t=
o
>> >> large AIC differences - meaning that having chosen a "base model" with=
out
>> >> employing covariates, I can't be sure that for a given covariate, anot=
her
>> >> base model would not yield better results.
>> >>
>> >> I suppose, although I am less sure, that a similar problem would occur=
if
>> >> I tried a stepwise addition of covariates instead of trialing all
>> >> combinations here. Having selected the best-performing covariate of th=
e
>> >> 1-covariate models and adding further covariates to this, I can't be s=
ure
>> >> that a 2+ combination with another first covariate would not yield a
>> >> better fit. For some data sets, using full permutation, I have already=
had
>> >> results where the best model had covariates ABC and the second-best
>> >> covariate D only - meaning that starting from a "best single covariate=
"
>> >> base (D), I would never have found the best model.
>> >>
>> >> I guess that one of these simplifying steps, or something similar, wil=
l be
>> >> necessary though unless I want to run tens of thousands of models. I w=
ould
>> >> be very grateful for some guidance from those who have performed analy=
ses
>> >> that were similarly in danger of inflation!
>> >>
>> >> best regards
>> >> florian weller
